newsitem.title: UK: Kvaerner plans Europe's tallest building in London.
newsitem.headline: Kvaerner plans Europe's tallest building in London.

text.p: Norway's Kvaerner ASA group Monday unveiled plans to build Europe's tallest building in the centre of the City of London financial district, but the project seems likely to run into delays.

Kvaerner subsidiary Trafalgar House wants the stunning 1,265-foot, 92-story Millenium Tower to be completed by 2001 to celebrate the turn of the century. The planned cost is 400 million pounds ($620 million).

"It is a statement of confidence in the city for the next century ... there is a tremendous spur to make this building a wonderful statement of excellence," architect Sir Norman Foster told a news conference.

"The thrill is to be able to do this in London and not travel to other end of the world to do it," he said, referring to the scarcity of tall buildings in central London compared to other major financial centres such as New York and Hong Kong.

Trafalgar House plans to erect the tower on the site of the Baltic Exchange, which was largely destroyed by an IRA bomb in 1992. The tower would dwarf Europe's tallest existing building, the 984-foot Commerzbank headquarters in Frankfurt.
Foster described the Millenium Tower as a continuous series of curves in different kinds of glass which would respond to the changing qualities of sunlight throughout the year.
Highlights include two 35,000-square-foot trading rooms as well as a number of luxury apartments in two separate towers at the top of the building.
The building would have 1.5 million square feet of space and room for 8,000 workers. A public viewing area 1,000 feet up would offer unparallelled views of the city.
"London is unique in the sense that it is one of very few cities where you cannot go to a higher level to gain a new perspective," Foster said.
Detailed studies showed that the tower would not obstruct views of existing highlights such as St. Paul's Cathedral, he added.
Alan Winter, managing director of Trafalgar House, said he would submit planning proposals next month and hoped to receive permission to start next April.

"We do not propose to build on speculation. A large part of the tower would have to be let to an anchor client before construction could start. We are in discussion with a number of possible clients," he said.
He gave no further details but made clear Kvaerner itself would not be an anchor client.
A spokeswoman for the Corporation of London, which will decide on planning permission, said Winter was unlikely to be able to stick to his timetable.
"Perhaps he's being a bit optimistic. Gaining permission could take a long time," she said by telephone.

Given likely protests about the size of the proposed tower, more than twice the height of the tallest existing building in the City of London -- the National Westminster Bank tower -- it seems likely there would first have to be a public inquiry which could delay the project by 18 months.
Trafalgar House will also have to gain permission from English Heritage, an agency charged with preserving buildings of architectural or historic interest and significance.
Last month, English Heritage said it was "skeptical" about the impact of the proposed skyscraper.
